questions.question: What motivated you to go on exchange? (pick the most important one) *
questions.answer: Explore new cultures

questions.question: Which aspects were crucial to choosing your study destination? *
questions.answer: I wanted to go somewhere far away and have somewhat of a culture shock while still being in a place where I could imagine myself living for several months. I'd heard great things about Seoul from friends that have stayed for a longer period of time, and I was not disappointed!

questions.question: How would you rate your overall study abroad experience? *
Additional comments:
How easy was it to find the information you needed to know upon arrival? *
questions.answer: I think the people at Yonsei were really good at sending emails with the necessary information when I first arrived. You do however have to keep up with the many emails they send, but as long as you stay organized it's really easy to find information about almost everything.

questions.question: What assistance, if any, did you receive when you arrived at your study destination? *
questions.answer: I asked for some help regarding the different course registration periods from the International Office of Affairs, and they were pretty fast to answer.

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the orientation and assistance available to students at your host institution upon arrival? *
Additional comments
questions.answer: I wish they were better at informing us about the social events in the beginning. I learned about the social gatherings at the on-campus orientation, and since it was a first-come, first-served registration, I missed out on the opportunity to sign up. I also only heard fromt the buddy/mentor program in November, towards the end of my stay, which is a bad unfortunate.

questions.question: How did you find housing? *
questions.answer: I found housing on my own

questions.question: Did you live on campus or off campus? *
questions.answer: Off campus

questions.question: How easy was it to find off campus housing? Any recommendations? *
questions.answer: I had heard of Simple Spaces through a friend of a friend, and found housing through them. The application process was really easy, and I ended up getting a shared apartment with two girls from Copenhagen. I can only recommend Simple Spaces since they offer nice apartments in some cool areas, and they arrange social events and trips for all their tenants. I met most of my new friends through Simple Spaces.

questions.question: What should future exchange students know about living off campus? *
questions.answer: I ended up living in Haebangchon, which is part of Itaewon. Even though it looks fairly close to Yonsei on the map, most days transportation took around an hour. Since attendance is mandatory, it is a good idea to consider whether or not you want to spend so much time on transport to get to and from uni almost every day. For me it wasn't a problem, since I got to live in a cool and interesting area. It did however also mean that whenever people from Yonsei would do something spontaneous in the Sinchon area around campus, I was often quite far away.

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the housing available to students? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: I didn't live on campus but I've heard it was allright.

questions.question: How easy did you find the registration process at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: It was quite easy to look through the course list, but since the only available list they give us before the semester starts is a year old, it meant that a lot of the courses I had planned to take, weren't available anymore, or had changed quite a bit. This made registration a bit stressful, since I had to rethink my courses and re-apply for pre-approval.

questions.question: Please describe the registration process at your host institution *
questions.answer: As I remember, there were several rounds. The first round is like a bidding system, where you have x points, and you give out the points according to which courses you want the most. Then you have a course add and drop period, where you can drop courses if you didn't like them and add new ones from the courses that still have spots open. Lastly there's a last round where you can only drop courses.

questions.question: What kind of help was available? *
questions.answer: I wrote a lot to the professors on the different courses with questions about the syllabus, workload etc., but you can also contact the International Office of Affairs or Yonsei Global on campus, where the have volunteers who can help answer questions.

questions.question: How successful were you in registering for the classes you wanted? *
questions.answer: In the first round I got all the courses I wanted. Unfortunately one of the courses wasn't at all what I thought it would be, and I tried signing up for Korean language, but failed. If you want to take a Korean class remember that you can only apply in the first bidding round because they have an assessment test in the first class. After that it's impossible to join, so I had to join another class which I ended up loving.

questions.question: What advice would you offer to future exchange students about registration at your host institution? *
questions.answer: Be prepared that some of the courses on the course list might not exist anymore. It's a good idea to have backups, if you don't get into the course you want. If you want to take Korean classes, don't be like me, and remember to apply in the first round!

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the academic programme at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: The academic level varied greatly between the courses I took. Some I found really challenging, while others were super easy.

questions.question: Were you a BA or MA student at UCPH when you were on exchange? *
questions.answer: BA

questions.question: Did you take BA or MA courses at your host university? *
questions.answer: Both

questions.question: Please elaborate on the level of courses *
questions.answer: I took 4 BA courses and one MA course accidentally, but the professor lightened up the syllabus for me, so I didn't have to read as many articles as the MA students.

questions.question: How did the style of teaching at your host institution compare with that of UCPH? *
questions.answer: A looot of lecture style classes, and not a lot of group discussions like at UCPH. I had to do quite a few in-class presentations, but other than that I spent most days in class just listening to the professor speak.

questions.question: How long were you on exchange? *
questions.answer: 1 semester

questions.question: Please list the courses you were enrolled in during your first semester. *
questions.answer: Intro to Korean Studies, Understanding K-pop, Korean Popular Culture and Korean Wave, Ecological Anthropology and The Two Koreas in Film and Literature

questions.question: What specific courses would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer: Honestly I would recommend all of them except Understanding K-pop, unless you are very into K-pop. Ecological Anthropology and The Two Koreas in Film and Literature were my favorite courses, and I've gotten the most out of them academically compared to the others.

What unexpected costs did you encounter? *
questions.answer: Nothing that I can think of.

questions.question: What items were more or less expensive than you expected? *
questions.answer: Food is less expensive than in Denmark, but still around 50-60 dkk. Even though it's generally more expensive to buy food at the grocery store, it is still possible to save some money and cook at home from time to time. Alcohol is crazy cheap as well as public transportation. Rent for an apartment is around the same price as Copenhagen, depending on the area you live in. Busses to visit other cities in Korea are quite cheap and easy to find, and I definitely recommend going on a few trips out of Seoul.

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the non-academic opportunities (clubs, sports, etc.) at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: I knew they were there, but there wasn't really any that caught my interest.

questions.question: What kinds of cultural, athletic and social activities were available for students at your host institution? *
questions.answer: Sports, dance, cooking, journalism, lgtbq+, photography etc. There were so many!

questions.question: Which non -academic activities would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer: I didn't join any, so unfortunately I don't have any recommendations.

questions.question: What do you recommend other visiting students see or do on their weekends or holidays? *
questions.answer: Go to the palaces, temples and museums in Seoul. Visit the parks! And definitely go on trips out of the city, especially if you enjoy spending time in nature. I can recommend Gyeongju, Jeonju and Sokcho! I also went on a Templestay, which is a fun, unique experience!

questions.question: How easy was it to adjust to the local culture of your exchange site? *
questions.answer: I had to get used to the fact that people bumped into me on the streets, and that nobody speaks on public transport. Other than that I thought it was pretty easy to adjust.

questions.question: Do you have any tips for socializing with local students?
questions.answer: Honestly I feel like the campus at Yonsei was very divided between the Korean students and the exchange students. Despite the clubs and mentor/buddy program, I dont really know how you could socialize.

questions.question: What, if any, cultural differences did you find particularly challenging? *
questions.answer:
Heavy drinking is pretty normal, especially during moments of socializing or bonding. I've definitely gotten drunk more and gone out way more compared to what I do in Denmark (although drinking is also a thing here lol). That being said no one is forcing you to drink, but I will say there is a lot of social pressure on the fact that everybody should get drunk together. 
Also, when you go to small local restaurants, they don't want people to spend a long time on their meal or by talking afterwards. Me and my friends have been rushed out of restaurants as soon as we finished eating a number of times.

questions.question: What parts of the culture did you most appreciate? *
questions.answer: I loved the food, the nightlife, the art and culture scene, the stark contrast between the traditional and the modern as well as the crazy, beautiful, never-sleeping chaos that is Seoul.

questions.question: What are the three most important things you would tell a UCPH student who is going to your host institution on exchange? *
questions.answer:
1. It is a big university, so it's easy to feel a bit small and anonymous. Make an effort in the beginning to find some friends to make everything seem a bit less overwhelming. 
2. Don't spend crazy amounts of time and energy on the assignments. I found that the level of requirement was a lot lower than what I'm used to. 
3. Even though the campus is nice, there's not a lot of spots outside of the library where you can study. There is however a lot of nice cafe's in Sinchon, where you can study in peace. My favorite was 'you want some', where you can sit in the window and look at the trees. Their insta handle is @cafe_youwantsome

questions.question: Is there any other information that you think might prove useful to future exchange students attending your host institution? *
questions.answer: Don't drown in the many deadlines. I found it useful to write everything down in one document, so I never lost track of when I had to submit different things

questions.question: What was the most rewarding part of your exchange experience? *
questions.answer: I learned so many things, not only through my classes at Yonsei but also through enjoying my time as a tourist there. It was amazing that every day I would go to class for some hours, and then have the option to spend the rest of the day exploring Seoul.

questions.question: What was the greatest challenge during the exchange? *
questions.answer: For me it was a little bit hard finding the balance between school and leisure time in the beginning. There were so many things I wanted to do and see during my stay, but I also felt a bit of pressure to keep up with the readings and assignments. I will say that even though the professors make it seem like they expect you to do everything and do it thoroughly, they still know that you are there on exchange and probably studying isn't your first priority. So enjoy your time exploring! Even though I accepted that I wouldn't be able to keep up with everything at uni, I still got fine grades in the end.

questions.question: Any other comments?
Do you agree to share your travel report with other fellow students? *
questions.answer: Yes
